they ought to have taken, they took <term>pyrite</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and various other materials in which there is no operation; these are expensive things from the shops, but in the labor they are of no value at all. Our material, however, is not bought from any shop, yet it is found daily in such a place, and merchants cast it into the streets. It is enough, therefore, that it is found for free. But the material of our <term>stone</term> <gloss>lapis</gloss> is compared to all those things with which the craftsmen labor. Indeed, our stone is <term>our salt</term>, <term>our Mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term> <gloss>aerugo</gloss>, <term>saltpeter</term> <gloss>halonitrum</gloss>, <term>sal ammoniac</term> <gloss>salmiacum</gloss>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulfur</term>, and infinite other things of that kind, yet it is not dug out from wild and rural mountains with hammers and other instruments. Our stone is extracted only from our mountains and springs; in our <term>Salt-spring</term> our <term>Salt</term> is found; from our earth our metal, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>sulfur</term> are poured, and not from wild, foreign, and rural mountains. The craftsmen do not understand all these things, nor can they believe or comprehend them; for the Lord has darkened and stopped up their senses, for which reason they have used these things otherwise than was proper, and have missed the mark entirely. Nevertheless, they persisted in that contrary sense and followed their own stubborn heads. For example, while they ought to have <term>distilled</term> gently, they <term>sublimed</term> with a strong fire, scorched <term>strong waters</term> <gloss>corrosive acids</gloss>, and immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, reducing them to nothing. Also, while they ought to have <term>dissolved</term> <gloss>solvere</gloss>, they <term>coagulated</term> there, and again, as men ignorant of things, they also treated the matter ignorantly. They fell into doubt and repeatedly claimed with lying words that the art was not true, but false, in which, however, they themselves are justly lying. For their own ignorance basely deceived them, which must be attributed to their own obscure and misty cunning, since, according to their own dark intellect, they interpreted words differently than they sounded. For example, while the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> (which they call grinding), those ignorant <term>Philosophasters</term> <gloss>pretenders to philosophy</gloss> understood it to mean burning, and they reduced things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. Likewise, when the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term> or transmute into water, then those <term>know-it-alls</term> <gloss>nasutuli</gloss> burned nature with <term>strong water</term> <gloss>acid</gloss>, and that same water, which has no...

<summary>The author distinguishes between common chemicals bought in shops and the true, free material of the Philosophers, criticizing ignorant pretenders for using excessive heat and corrosive acids.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, sulfur, mercury, salt, calcination, distillation, Philosophastros, strong water, corrosive acids, secret matter</keywords>
